newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's Monti defends plans to raise energy taxes.
newsitem.headline: EU's Monti defends plans to raise energy taxes.

text.p: European Union single market and taxation chief Mario Monti defended on Tuesday controversial plans to raise minimum taxes on motor and heating fuels and extend it to electricity and natural gas.
Monti said the move was not aimed at increasing taxes as it should be accompanied by equivalent reductions in labour taxes.
"This is not a new tax," he told a seminar organised by Brussels-based think tank Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS).

"This simply aims at providing member states with a concrete possibility to implement the restructuring of their taxation by taxing more energy and, in a principle of tax neutrality, reducing somewhat correspondingly, non-wage costs," he said.

He also stressed that the proposal, expected to be discussed at the Commission's regular meeting next week, had been requested by EU heads of state after a failure to agree on a tax to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
The draft proposal foresees an EU-wide minimum tax on motor diesel of 310 European currency units per 1,000 litres in 1998, rising to 343 Ecus in 2000 and 393 Ecus in 2002.
Petrol would be taxed a minimum 417 Ecus in 1998, increasing to 450 Ecus in 2000 and 500 Ecus in 2002.
Although the proposed minima in most cases are below the actual rates in the 15-nation EU, the European industry fears they will set the trend for future tax rises.
Monti said the texts had been revised to stress that the new rates would not increase the overall tax burden in the EU.

This could be achieved if national governments agreed to use any additional tax revenue to lower salary-linked contributions to social security systems, effectively fulfilling their promise to reduce unemployment.
"I'm confident it will be perceived for what it is after so much lip service paid by everyone to the need to help employment in Europe," he said.
But he recognised that there were limits to what the Commission could do to make sure this happened. Direct taxation and labour charges are a matter for national governments alone.
He said the draft had also taken care to protect Europe's industrial competitiveness, especially regarding energy intensive sectors, which would benefit from reduced rates.
The proposal was tentatively on the agenda for the Commission's weekly meeting on Wednesday, but top aides of the EU's 20 commissioners decided to remove it rather than risk a political row.
European Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann opposes it, a position reflecting the one held among European industrial sectors such as chemicals, cement and carmaking.

Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy also voiced concern over its impact on nuclear electricity, which would be taxed for the first time, while the executive's two Spanish commissioners are worried about a possible resumption of a damaging lorry strike in their country.
